title: Quillpath SaaS Starter Plan Pricing
prompt: Our client is Quillpath, a US software company. It sells cloud software that small home-services businesses — plumbers, landscapers, cleaners — use to schedule jobs, send quotes and get paid. Customers pay monthly and can cancel at any time. For years Quillpath sold one plan, Pro, at $100 a month. In January 2025 it launched a cheaper Starter plan at $40 a month, with fewer features and a single user. New customers per month nearly tripled. Quillpath's board has a rule: each type of customer should be worth at least three times what it costs to acquire. The CFO says Starter fails that test and wants to shut it down; the head of growth wants to keep it. The CEO has asked us what Quillpath should do with the Starter plan.
interviewerNotes: Source: AI Casing Case 05 (v1.0, Oct 2026), interviewer-led mode. Hard: three quantitative steps. Standalone: Pro margin $80 ÷ 2% churn = $4,000 LTV vs. $1,200 CAC (3.3×); Starter margin $30 ÷ 5% churn (not 6% — the 1% who upgraded didn't leave) = $600 vs. $300 (2.0×) — the CFO is right on that narrow basis. But 20% of Starter customers upgrade to Pro: $600 + 20% × $4,000 = $1,400 (4.7×), net $1,100. Starter also takes ~150 Pro sign-ups a month (500 → 350). A month of sign-ups: Pro only 500 × $2,800 = $1.40M; with Starter 350 × $2,800 + 1,000 × $1,100 = $2.08M (+$0.68M; the CFO's standalone view gives $1.28M). Cannibalization breakeven ≈ 390 Pro a month. Price test at $60: Starter value $50 × 20 + $800 − $300 = $1,500 net; 400 × $2,800 + 800 × $1,500 = $2.32M (+$0.24M). But the test ran 8 weeks: it holds unless Starter churn rises above ~7% a month or upgrades fall below 12.5%. Recommendation: keep Starter, move new customers to $60, keep the ~9,000 existing customers at $40, and watch churn and upgrades. An 'extend the test first' answer is acceptable if the +$0.24M at stake is quantified. Release order in the guide: Exhibits 1 and 2 together (either order) → Exhibit 3 (sign-ups by plan, any time after the structure) → Exhibit 4 (price test) only after the upgrade-adjusted value is worked out. The case has no brainstorm module; feature or packaging ideas are credited under creativity.

dataLedger.label: The product
dataLedger.value: Quillpath's product is cloud software for scheduling, quotes, invoicing and payments, used by small home-services businesses in the US.

dataLedger.label: Difference between the plans
dataLedger.value: Pro has all features, unlimited users, team scheduling and reports; Starter has one user and core scheduling and invoicing only; both are billed monthly.

dataLedger.label: How customers sign up
dataLedger.value: Most Pro customers have a demo with a salesperson first, while Starter customers sign up online on their own.

dataLedger.label: What "worth three times the acquisition cost" means
dataLedger.spoken: what the board's three-times rule means
dataLedger.value: Under the board's rule, lifetime value — the gross margin earned over a customer's life — divided by the cost to acquire that customer has to be at least 3.

dataLedger.label: Company size
dataLedger.value: Quillpath has about 20,000 paying customers today.

dataLedger.label: Market growth
dataLedger.value: Demand for small-business software is growing about 10% a year.

dataLedger.label: What the CEO cares about
dataLedger.value: The CEO's goal is to create as much long-term value as possible from new customers while respecting the board's rule.

dataLedger.label: Plan economics: monthly price and cost to serve, Pro and Starter
dataLedger.value: Pro is $100 a month with a $20 monthly cost to serve, and Starter is $40 a month with a $10 monthly cost to serve — hosting, support and payment processing.

dataLedger.label: Customer acquisition cost (CAC), Pro and Starter
dataLedger.value: The cost to acquire one new customer is $1,200 for Pro, through a sales demo, and $300 for Starter, which is self-serve, and it does not change with volume.

dataLedger.label: How lifetime value is calculated
dataLedger.value: Lifetime value is monthly gross margin times expected lifetime in months; expected lifetime is about 1 divided by the monthly cancellation rate, and gross margin is price minus cost to serve.

dataLedger.label: Pro cohort retention (customers who signed up January–March 2025)
dataLedger.value: Of the 1,050 Pro customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 98.0% were still on Pro after month 1, 94.1% after month 3, 88.6% after month 6 and 78.5% after month 12, so 2.0%, 5.9%, 11.4% and 21.5% had cancelled by those months.

dataLedger.label: Starter cohort status: still on Starter, upgraded to Pro, cancelled
dataLedger.value: Of the 3,000 Starter customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 94% were still on Starter after month 1, 82% after month 3, 65% after month 6 and 40% after month 12; by those months 1%, 5%, 11% and 20% had upgraded to Pro and were still customers, and 5%, 13%, 24% and 40% had cancelled.

dataLedger.label: Cohort notes: steady cancellation, upgrade timing, how finance values upgrades
dataLedger.value: Cancellation rates have stayed roughly steady from month to month, very few Starter customers upgrade after month 12, upgraded customers then behave like Pro customers, and finance values a Starter sign-up at its Starter LTV plus one Pro LTV for each customer who upgrades.

dataLedger.label: New customers per month by plan, before and after Starter launched
dataLedger.spoken: new customers per month by plan
dataLedger.value: New customers per month were 500 Pro in 2024, before Starter launched, and 350 Pro plus 1,000 Starter — 1,350 in total — from January 2025 to June 2026.

dataLedger.label: Starter price test results: sign-ups per month at each test price
dataLedger.value: In the eight-week price test, sign-ups per month were 350 Pro and 1,000 Starter at a $40 Starter price, and 400 Pro and 800 Starter at $60, scaled to Quillpath's full website traffic.

dataLedger.label: Price test notes: costs unchanged, churn and upgrades not yet measurable
dataLedger.spoken: the notes on the price test
dataLedger.value: Starter's cost to serve ($10 a month) and acquisition cost ($300) are the same at either price, and cancellation and upgrade rates for customers who signed up at $60 can't be measured yet because the test lasted only eight weeks.

dataLedger.label: When customers upgrade
dataLedger.value: Most upgrades are between months 3 and 9, usually when the business hires its first employee; very few are after month 12.

dataLedger.label: Why Pro sign-ups fell
dataLedger.value: Pro marketing spend, the sales team and demo requests were unchanged, and in interviews most people who'd have bought Pro said they chose Starter to save money.

dataLedger.label: Who buys each plan
dataLedger.value: Starter buyers are mostly one-person businesses, and Pro buyers mostly have three or more staff.

dataLedger.label: Competitors' entry-plan prices
dataLedger.value: The main competitors' entry plans are $50–$70 a month.

dataLedger.label: How the price test worked
dataLedger.value: For eight weeks, website visitors were randomly shown Starter at $40 or $60, results are scaled to Quillpath's full traffic, and churn and upgrade rates for $60 customers can't be measured yet.

dataLedger.label: Existing Starter customers
dataLedger.value: About 9,000 customers are on Starter at $40 today, and a new price could apply to new customers only.

exhibits.interpretationKey: At $60: Starter margin $50, standalone LTV $1,000, plus $800 of upgrade value, net $1,500 per sign-up; 400 × $2,800 + 800 × $1,500 = $2.32M vs. $2.08M at $40 (+$0.24M, +12%) — fewer Starter sign-ups, each worth more, and 50 more customers choose Pro; $60 is inside competitors' $50–$70. structureKey: A strong structure frames a product-line pricing decision: per-customer economics by plan (price, cost to serve, how long customers stay, acquisition cost → LTV and LTV/CAC); how the plans interact — Starter customers upgrading to Pro (good) and Starter taking sales from Pro (bad); the options (keep at $40, change the price, change the features, shut it down); and the market (competitor prices, what small businesses will pay). Strong candidates question the CFO's test up front (a plan can fail the ratio and still be worth having if it feeds Pro), name both interaction effects before seeing data, set the goal as total value created, and mention existing Starter customers if the price changes. Red flags: treating the plans as independent, only growth or only the ratio, generic frameworks.
recommendationKey: Keep Starter, and raise its price to $60 for new customers. On its own a Starter customer is worth $600 against a $300 acquisition cost (2.0×) — the CFO is right on that narrow basis. But 20% of Starter customers upgrade to Pro; counting that, a Starter sign-up is worth $1,400 (4.7×). Starter also takes about 150 Pro sign-ups a month; netting both, a month of sign-ups is worth about $2.08M with Starter vs. $1.40M with Pro only (+$0.68M). The $60 price test lifts that to $2.32M (+$0.24M a month) — but the test ran only 8 weeks: it holds unless Starter churn rises above ~7% a month or upgrades fall below 12.5%. Roll out $60 to new customers only, keep the ~9,000 current Starter customers at $40, and track churn and upgrades closely for six months. Acceptable alternative: keep $40 and extend the test, if the +$0.24M at stake is quantified and weighed against the risk.
